item.title: C# Method Group Conversion Explained: Why Parentheses Matter
item.description:
“C# Method Group Conversion Explained: Why Parentheses Matter”

When you reference a method name without following it with parentheses—for instance, referencing SomeObject.MethodName instead of SomeObject.MethodName()—the compiler interprets this reference as a method group. This terminology signifies a potential collection of methods.

The Nature of the Method Group

A method group arises primarily because of method overloading. A single name can represent several methods with different signatures (like ToString() vs. ToString(string format)).

item.title: C# Event Handling: Demystifying Delegates and Event Signatures
item.description:
“C# Event Handling: Demystifying Delegates and Event Signatures”

How do C# events operate internally, and what is the fundamental role of delegates in enabling this mechanism? The interaction between an event and its associated handler methods hinges entirely on the delegate’s definition, which specifies the required method signature.

The Delegate: A Method Reference Contract

A delegate in C# functions as a type-safe reference, or pointer, to one or more methods. This abstraction allows methods to be treated and passed around like any other variable.
